content.overview: BNS s. 26 — Act not intended to cause death, done by consent in good faith for person's benefit.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Act not intended to cause death, done by consent in good faith for person's benefit. BNS restatement of IPC 88. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 88. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 26 is the rule on “Act not intended to cause death, done by consent in good faith for person's benefit”. The section provides that nothing, which is not intended to cause death, is an offence by reason of any harm which it may cause, or be intended by the doer to cause, or be known by the doer to be likely to cause, to any person for whose benefit it is done in good faith, and who has given a consent, whether express or implied, to suffer that harm, or to take the risk of that harm. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 26 exists so that “Act not intended to cause death, done by consent in good faith for person's benefit” has a closed legal test in Chapter III — General Exceptions. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: When an act is not an offence: mistake, accident, infancy, unsoundness, consent, compulsion — and the right of private defence.

The provision in detail
26. Nothing, which is not intended to cause death, is an offence by reason of any harm which it may cause, or be intended by the doer to cause, or be known by the doer to be likely to cause, to any person for whose benefit it is done in good faith, and who has given a consent, whether express or implied, to suffer that harm, or to take the risk of that harm

Essential ingredients
1. Nothing, which is not intended to cause death, is an offence by reason of any harm which it may cause, or be intended by the doer to cause, or be known by the doer to be likely to cause, to any person for whose benefit it is done in good faith, and who has given a consent, whether express or implied, to suffer that harm, or to take the risk of that harm

Statutory illustrations
Illustration (a). A, a surgeon, knowing that a particular operation is likely to cause the death of Z, who suffers under the painful complaint, but not intending to cause Z’s death, and intending, in good faith, Z’s benefit, performs that operation on Z, with Z’s consent. A has committed no offence

Exam use: quote illustration (a), then write which ingredient of BNS s. 26 it proves. Copying the illustration without that mapping sentence does not score.

hypotheticals.analysis:
Step 1 — Identify the provision. The correct current-law cite is BNS s. 26 (Act not intended to cause death, done by consent in good faith for person's benefit), Chapter III — General Exceptions.
Step 2 — State the legal test in your own words, then list the ingredients:
   (1) Nothing, which is not intended to cause death, is an offence by reason of any harm which it may cause, or be intended by the doer to cause, or be known by the doer to be likely to cause, to any person for whose benefit it is done in good faith, and who has given a consent, whether express or implied, to suffer that harm, or to take the risk of that harm
Step 3 — Check limitations, provisos and the rest of the Chapter so you do not apply s. 26 in a vacuum.
Step 4 — Map each fact to an ingredient. Write “this fact proves ingredient (a)” or “this fact is missing, so the section is not made out”.
Step 5 — Conclude. If every essential ingredient is proved and no exception covers the case, BNS s. 26 applies. If any essential ingredient fails, say so and stop. Do not invent a different section to save the answer.

learningObjectives: Understand the medical/surgical exception under BNS s. 26.
Analyze the requirement of good faith, personal benefit, and express/implied consent.
Identify the statutory limit: the act must not be intended to cause death.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 26 provides that nothing which is not intended to cause death, is an offence by reason of any harm which it may cause, or be intended by the doer to cause, or be known by the doer to be likely to cause, to any person for whose benefit it is done in good faith, and who has given a consent, whether express or implied, to suffer that harm, or to take the risk of that harm.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: A person acting in good faith for another's benefit with their consent is protected from criminal liability for harm caused, provided death is not intentionally caused. This forms the primary penal shield for surgical and medical procedures.
statutoryFramework: Chapter III — General Exceptions, BNS s. 26 (corresponding to IPC s. 88).
Threshold condition: Act must be done 'for the benefit' of the person in 'good faith'.
Harm limit: Must NOT be intended to cause death; risk of grievous hurt or even known likelihood of death is permitted if not intentionally caused.
Consent requirement: Requires express or implied consent from the person suffering the harm.
Explanation to s. 27/s. 26: Mere pecuniary benefit is not 'benefit' within the meaning of this section.
essentialIngredients: The act was done for the benefit of the person who suffered the harm.
The act was done in good faith (due care and attention under BNS s. 2(11)).
The person gave consent (express or implied) to suffer the harm or run the risk.
The doer did not intend to cause death.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 26 provides crucial protection for surgeons, physicians, and individuals rendering dangerous but necessary aid with consent. Unlike s. 25 (which prohibits even knowledge of likelihood of grievous hurt), s. 26 permits procedures known to carry grave risks (such as open-heart surgery, amputation, or experimental therapy) because the act is performed in good faith for the patient's therapeutic benefit with their consent. The only absolute prohibition is the intentional infliction of death. 'Benefit' does not mean mere financial gain; it denotes physical, mental, or personal well-being.
examples: Teaching example (Surgeon operating): A qualified surgeon, knowing an advanced surgical procedure carries a 40% mortality risk, explains the risk to an adult patient suffering from a fatal tumor. The patient signs informed consent. During the operation, the patient dies without surgical negligence. Section 26 protects the surgeon.

Teaching example (Pecuniary gain excluded): An individual consents to have his kidney removed solely to sell it for money. The doctor cannot claim s. 26 because pecuniary gain is not 'benefit' under the penal law.
distinctions: Section 25 vs Section 26: Section 25 excludes even knowledge of likelihood of death or grievous hurt (sports/games). Section 26 permits known risk of death/grievous hurt provided death is not intended and the act is for the person's benefit.
Section 26 vs Section 30: Section 26 requires consent; Section 30 operates in emergencies where consent is impossible to obtain.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether a surgeon who performed an urgent complex surgery with the patient's consent is liable for culpable homicide when the patient dies of surgical shock.
Rule: Section 26 protects acts done in good faith for person's benefit with consent, provided death was not intended.

Application: Check if informed consent was obtained, whether the procedure was medically indicated (for patient's benefit), whether the surgeon acted with due care and attention, and verify absence of intentional killing.
Conclusion: If medical benefit, good faith, and consent are proved without intent to kill, s. 26 applies.

shortAnswer: State BNS s. 26 text on acts done in good faith for benefit with consent.
Highlight the surgical shield: death must not be intended, but known risk of death is protected.
Note that pecuniary benefit is excluded.

Death must not be intentionally caused.
Act must be in good faith for the physical or personal benefit of the patient.
